{{Short description|Theorem relating unitary operators to one-parameter Lie groups}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Stone's theorem''' on [[one-parameter group|one-parameter]] [[unitary group]]s is a basic theorem of [[functional analysis]] that establishes a one-to-one correspondence between [[self-adjoint operator]]s on a [[Hilbert space]] <math>\mathcal{H}</math> and one-parameter families

:<math>(U_{t})_{t \in \R}</math>

of [[unitary operator]]s that are strongly continuous, i.e.,

:<math>\forall t_0 \in \R, \psi \in \mathcal{H}: \qquad \lim_{t \to t_0} U_t(\psi) = U_{t_0}(\psi),</math>

and are homomorphisms, i.e.,

:<math>\forall s,t \in \R : \qquad U_{t + s} = U_t U_s.</math>

Such one-parameter families are ordinarily referred to as '''strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups'''.

The theorem was proved by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Marshall Stone|first=Marshall|last=Stone|year1=1930|year2=1932}}, and {{harvs|txt|authorlink=John von Neumann|first=John|last=von Neumann|year=1932}} showed that the requirement that <math>(U_t)_{t \in \R}</math> be strongly continuous can be relaxed to say that it is merely [[weakly measurable function | weakly measurable]], at least when the Hilbert space is [[separable space | separable]].

This is an impressive result, as it allows one to define the [[derivative]] of the [[map (mathematics) | mapping]] <math>t \mapsto U_t,</math> which is only supposed to be [[continuous function | continuous]]. It is also related to the theory of [[Lie group]]s and [[Lie algebra]]s.

== Formal statement ==
The statement of the theorem is as follows.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2013}} Theorem 10.15</ref> 

:'''Theorem.''' Let <math>(U_t)_{t \in \R}</math> be a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group. Then there exists a unique (possibly unbounded) operator <math>A: \mathcal{D}_A \to \mathcal{H}</math>, that is self-adjoint on <math>\mathcal{D}_A</math> and such that
::<math>\forall t \in \R : \qquad U_t = e^{itA}.</math> 
:The domain of <math>A</math> is defined by 
::<math>\mathcal{D}_A = \left \{ \psi \in \mathcal{H} \left | \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{-i}{\varepsilon} \left(U_{\varepsilon} (\psi) - \psi \right) \text{ exists} \right. \right \}.</math>
:Conversely, let <math>A: \mathcal{D}_A \to \mathcal{H}</math> be a (possibly unbounded) self-adjoint operator on <math>\mathcal{D}_A \subseteq \mathcal{H}.</math> Then the one-parameter family <math>(U_{t})_{t \in \R}</math> of unitary operators defined by 
::<math>\forall t \in \R : \qquad U_{t} := e^{itA}</math>
:is a strongly continuous one-parameter group.

In both parts of the theorem, the expression <math>e^{itA}</math> is defined by means of the [[functional calculus]], which uses the [[spectral theorem]] for unbounded [[self-adjoint operator]]s. 

The operator <math>A</math> is called the '''infinitesimal generator''' of <math>(U_{t})_{t \in \R}.</math> Furthermore, <math>A</math> will be a bounded operator if and only if the operator-valued mapping <math>t \mapsto U_{t}</math> is [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]]-continuous.

The infinitesimal generator <math>A</math> of a strongly continuous unitary group <math>(U_{t})_{t \in \R}</math> may be computed as

:<math>A\psi = -i\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{U_\varepsilon\psi-\psi}{\varepsilon},</math>

with the domain of <math>A</math> consisting of those vectors <math>\psi</math> for which the limit exists in the norm topology. That is to say, <math>A</math> is equal to <math>-i</math> times the derivative of <math>U_t</math> with respect to <math>t</math> at <math>t=0</math>. Part of the statement of the theorem is that this derivative exists—i.e., that <math>A</math> is a densely defined self-adjoint operator. The result is not obvious even in the finite-dimensional case, since <math>U_t</math> is only assumed (ahead of time) to be continuous, and not differentiable.

== Example ==

The family of translation operators

:<math>\left[ T_t(\psi) \right](x) = \psi(x + t)</math>

is a one-parameter unitary group of unitary operators; the infinitesimal generator of this family is an [[extensions of symmetric operators|extension]] of the differential operator

:<math>-i \frac{d}{dx}</math>

defined on the space of continuously differentiable complex-valued functions with [[compact support]] on <math>\R.</math> Thus

:<math>T_{t} = e^{t \frac{d}{dx}}.</math>

In other words, motion on the line is generated by the [[momentum operator]].

== Applications ==

Stone's theorem has numerous applications in [[quantum mechanics]]. For instance, given an isolated quantum mechanical system, with Hilbert space of states {{mvar|H}}, [[time evolution]] is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group on <math>\mathcal{H}</math>. The infinitesimal generator of this group is the system [[Hamiltonian (quantum theory)|Hamiltonian]].

{{further|Stone–von Neumann theorem|Heisenberg group}}

==Using Fourier transform==

Stone's Theorem can be recast using the language of the [[Fourier transform]]. The real line <math>\R</math> is a locally compact abelian group. Non-degenerate *-representations of the [[group algebra of a locally compact group|group C*-algebra]] <math>C^*(\R)</math> are in one-to-one correspondence with strongly continuous unitary representations of <math>\R,</math> i.e., strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups. On the other hand, the Fourier transform is a *-isomorphism from <math>C^*(\R)</math> to <math>C_0(\R),</math> the <math>C^*</math>-algebra of continuous complex-valued functions on the real line that vanish at infinity. Hence, there is a one-to-one correspondence between strongly continuous one-parameter unitary groups and *-representations of <math>C_0(\R).</math> As every *-representation of <math>C_0(\R)</math> corresponds uniquely to a self-adjoint operator, Stone's Theorem holds.

Therefore, the procedure for obtaining the infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group is as follows:

* Let <math>(U_{t})_{t \in \R}</math> be a strongly continuous unitary representation of <math>\R</math> on a [[Hilbert space]] <math>\mathcal{H}</math>.
* Integrate this unitary representation to yield a non-degenerate *-representation <math>\rho</math> of <math>C^*(\R)</math> on <math>\mathcal{H}</math> by first defining <math display="block">\forall f \in C_c(\R): \quad \rho(f) := \int_{\R} f(t) ~ U_{t} dt,</math> and then extending <math>\rho</math> to all of <math>C^*(\R)</math> by continuity.
* Use the Fourier transform to obtain a non-degenerate *-representation <math>\tau</math> of <math>C_0(\R )</math> on <math>\mathcal{H}</math>.
* By the [[Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem|Riesz-Markov Theorem]], <math>\tau</math> gives rise to a [[projection-valued measure]] on <math>\R</math> that is the resolution of the identity of a unique [[self-adjoint operator]] <math>A</math>, which may be unbounded.
* Then <math>A</math> is the infinitesimal generator of <math>(U_{t})_{t \in \R }.</math>

The precise definition of <math>C^*(\R)</math> is as follows. Consider the *-algebra <math>C_c(\R),</math> the continuous complex-valued functions on <math>\R</math> with compact support, where the multiplication is given by [[convolution]]. The completion of this *-algebra with respect to the <math>L^1</math>-norm is a Banach *-algebra, denoted by <math>(L^1(\R),\star).</math> Then <math>C^*(\R)</math> is defined to be the '''enveloping <math>C^*</math>-algebra''' of <math>(L^1(\R),\star)</math>, i.e., its completion with respect to the largest possible <math>C^*</math>-norm. It is a non-trivial fact that, via the Fourier transform, <math>C^*(\R)</math> is isomorphic to <math>C_0(\R).</math> A result in this direction is the [[Riemann–Lebesgue lemma|Riemann-Lebesgue Lemma]], which says that the Fourier transform maps <math>L^1(\R)</math> to <math>C_0(\R).</math>

== Generalizations ==

The [[Stone–von Neumann theorem]] generalizes Stone's theorem to a ''pair'' of self-adjoint operators, <math>(P,Q)</math>, satisfying the [[canonical commutation relation]], and shows that these are all unitarily equivalent to the [[position operator]] and [[momentum operator]] on <math>L^2(\R).</math>

The [[Hille–Yosida theorem]] generalizes Stone's theorem to strongly continuous [[C0-semigroup|one-parameter semigroups]] of [[contraction (operator theory)|contraction]]s on [[Banach space]]s.
